sections.body: Networks connect devices. The internet uses protocols like TCP/IP to route packets. DNS translates names (example.org) into IP addresses.
ENCRYPTION scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. HTTPS encrypts traffic between your browser and websites (look for the padlock).
Public-key cryptography uses a pair of keys: a public key to encrypt (or verify) and a private key to decrypt (or sign). It lets strangers communicate securely.
Common attacks: phishing, malware, weak passwords, unpatched software. Defences: updates, 2FA, backups and caution.

options: Translates website names into IP addresses
hints: Computers find each other by numbers.
A contacts app turns a friend's name into their phone number. DNS does something similar for websites.
quiz.explain: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.

quiz.q: In public-key encryption, which key must be kept secret?
hints: One key is shared with everyone.
A mailbox slot (public) lets anyone drop letters in; only the owner's key (private) opens it.
quiz.explain: The private key must stay secret; the public key can be shared.
